Recovery Guarantees for Continual Learning of Dependent Tasks: Memory, Data-Dependent Regularization, and Data-Dependent Weights

 

Liangzu Peng∗          Uday Kiran Reddy Tadipatri∗          Ziqing Xu          Eric Eaton       René Vidal

University of Pennsylvania

††footnotetext: ∗: Equal contribution.
Abstract

Continual learning (CL) is concerned with learning multiple tasks sequentially without forgetting previously learned tasks. Despite substantial empirical advances over recent years, the theoretical development of CL remains in its infancy. At the heart of developing CL theory lies the challenge that the data distribution varies across tasks, and we argue that properly addressing this challenge requires understanding this variation–dependency among tasks. To explicitly model task dependency, we consider nonlinear regression tasks and propose the assumption that these tasks are dependent in such a way that the data of the current task is a nonlinear transformation of previous data. With this model and under natural assumptions, we prove statistical recovery guarantees (more specifically, bounds on estimation errors) for several CL paradigms in practical use, including experience replay with data-independent regularization and data-independent weights that balance the losses of tasks, replay with data-dependent weights, and continual learning with data-dependent regularization (e.g., knowledge distillation). To the best of our knowledge, our bounds are informative in cases where prior work gives vacuous bounds.

1 Introduction

Continual learning (CL) aims to learn multiple tasks presented sequentially, with a key goal to address the situation of catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989): learning new tasks risks performance degradation on previously learned tasks. To reduce forgetting, memory-based methods store some past data, to be used with new data for training the new task (Robins, 1993; Shin et al., 2017; Aljundi et al., 2019; Dokania et al., 2019; Prabhu et al., 2020; Verwimp et al., 2021; Bang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022); regularization-based methods optimize the current task with a regularization term that encourages proximity to the model previously learned (Li and Hoiem, 2017; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Zenke et al., 2017; Rebuffi et al., 2017; Park et al., 2019; Buzzega et al., 2020); constrained optimization methods enforce non-forgetting requirements as optimization constraints while solving the current task (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017; Chaudhry et al., 2019; Peng et al., 2023a; Elenter et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

In contrast to the abundance of empirical advances, theoretical investigations in CL are relatively scarce. Existing theoretical contributions are of at least two types. The first type considers linear models or the kernel regime (Bennani and Sugiyama, 2020; Doan et al., 2021; Heckel, 2022; Evron et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Swartworth et al., 2023; Goldfarb et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024; Banayeeanzade et al., 2025; Evron et al., 2025). With such specific settings, it is possible to derive meaningful and even tight bounds, but the resulting theory might not apply to existing CL methods that are specifically designed for deep networks or general nonlinear models. The other type of work considers general models (e.g., within a PAC-Bayes framework or based on the Rademacher complexity) (Pentina and Lampert, 2015; Yin et al., 2020; Ye and Bors, 2022; Friedman and Meir, 2024). With such general settings, it is possible to derive CL guarantees by leveraging tools from classic (PAC) learning theory (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014; Mohri et al., 2018; Alquier and others, 2024), but the resulting theory often fails to capture the benefits of learning multiple tasks sequentially, or the resulting bound does not necessarily tend to zero even in the presence of infinitely many samples.

In light of the above, we are motivated to seek a middle ground that combines the best of both worlds: derive meaningful error bounds for general nonlinear models and commonly used CL paradigms.

Importance of Task Dependency. We argue that attaining the above goal requires modeling how tasks are related to each other. We illustrate this by way of examples.

Example 1.

The error bounds (specifically, generalization bounds) of Ye and Bors (2022); Friedman and Meir (2024); Mansour et al. (2009) grow linearly with the “distance” between the data distributions of two tasks. For two zero-mean Gaussian distributions with variances 11 and s2s^{2}, respectively, this distance is proportional to |s2−1||s^{2}-1|, and thus grows unbounded as ss increases (cf. Remark 3). These are two basic distributions related in a simple way, i.e., one is a scalar multiple of the other, yet the bound depending linearly on s2s^{2} becomes vacuous even for a mildly large ss.

Example 2.

In the work of Peng et al. (2023a), the data within each task are i.i.d., and data across tasks are dependent. The proof of Peng et al. (2023a) reduces from a complicated CL situation to the standard scenario of learning a single task from i.i.d. data. As a side effect of this reduction, the bound of every task in Peng et al. (2023a) depends logarithmically on the total number TT of seen tasks and thus worsens as TT grows; this is somehow counterintuitive as it indicates learning more tasks enlarges the error bound of every task. In hindsight, analyzing dependent data appears to be intractable under the general setting of Peng et al. (2023a) as they do not specify how the tasks depend on each other. This leaves open the challenge of identifying task dependency that avoids degrading, or ideally improves, continual learning performance.

The Proposed CL Model With Task Dependency. In order to address issues pertaining to Examples 1 and 2 and to furthermore develop meaningful error bounds, we propose a CL framework with explicit modeling of task dependency. Specifically, we consider the problem of continual noisy nonlinear regression: learn a function f∗f^{*} from a sequence of noisy nonlinear regression tasks with f∗f^{*} assumed to be the shared true predictor of all these tasks. This is a setting that generalizes previous works on continual linear regression to the nonlinear, noisy case. Recognizing that directly analyzing such continual nonlinear regression model might lead to unsatisfactory bounds (Examples 1 and 2), we then arm this model with task dependency, which posits that the data of the present task are obtained as a nonlinear yet unknown transformation of the data from previous tasks. This task dependency is motivated from several perspectives (Section 2.2). For example, it draws inspiration from the rotated MNIST and permuted MNIST datasets that have benchmarked many fundamental CL methods; there, the transformation is either some rotation or permutation. Also, it finds inspiration from dynamical systems, where the current state is obtained as a transformation of the previous state.

Implications of Our CL Model and Task Dependency. We now sketch how the issues in Examples 1 and 2 are resolved with the proposed model and task dependency. For the two tasks in Example 1, the nonlinear transformation is simply a scaling function that multiplies its input by ss; and ss is the Lipschitz constant of this transformation. Crucially, we find that all our theorems exhibit only a logarithmic dependency on ss in the context of Example 1, thereby allowing ss to grow polynomially with problem size (e.g., dimension, sample size), without drastically affecting our bounds. This is a significant improvement over the linear dependency of s2s^{2} in Example 1 (Mansour et al., 2009; Ye and Bors, 2022; Friedman and Meir, 2024).

Unlike Example 2, our task dependency assumption makes the analysis tractable, though still non-trivial (cf. Fig. 2). In particular, it enables us to prove concentration bounds for dependent data, and it suffices to apply the bounds only once. By doing so, we eliminate the logarithmic dependency on TT as discussed in Example 2 where the concentration inequalities are invoked TT times.

More importantly, the proposed model and task dependency allow us to develop theoretical guarantees under a unifying framework and in a systematic fashion. Under basic assumptions, we bound the estimation errors of recovering f∗f^{*} for the aforementioned CL paradigms, including memory-based methods, regularization-based methods, and constrained optimization methods. In more detail:

  • •

    We begin by analyzing weighted experience replay with data-independent regularizers, where the weights balance contributions of each task (Section 3.2). With a non-uniform choice of weights, our bound on the weighted estimation error is inversely proportional to the total number of available data; such a bound is optimal. With uniform weights, our bound is also optimal if the replay buffer stores a constant fraction of the full data of each task.

  • •

    Then, we analyze regularization-based methods with a knowledge distillation regularizer (Section 3.3). While such regularizer is data-dependent, we can still prove estimation error bounds via a non-trivial recursive argument, resulting in improvements over prior work in terms of generality (Heckel, 2022; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025) and tightness (Yin et al., 2020) (cf. Remark 5).

  • •

    Lastly, we draw motivations from the constrained learning framework (Chamon et al., 2022; Elenter et al., 2023) and derive error bounds for replay with data-dependent weights, where the weights might now be thought of as dual variables in primal dual optimization (Section 3.4). We obtain error bounds of a similar flavor by extending our previous results to account for the fact that the weights are now random variables as well, depending on the data.

2 Problem Setup

In Section 2.1, we introduce our data model with the task dependency specified in an autoregressive fashion, based upon which we will develop our theorems. In Section 2.2 we provide justifications and motivations on our proposed task dependency model.

2.1 Data Model, Task Dependency, and Samples

Data Model with Autoregressive Task Dependency. Let TT be the number of tasks seen thus far. Let [T]:={1,…,T}[T]:=\{1,\dots,T\}. We consider a nonlinear regression setting, where each task tt shares a true predictor f∗:ℝdx→ℝdyf^{*}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} that maps input xtx_{t} to output yty_{t} up to some random noise vtv_{t}, similarly to prior work (Evron et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Elenter et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025). In addition, we specify the task dependency in an autoregressive manner through some deterministic, nonlinear transformation gt:ℝ(t−1)×dx→ℝdxg_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{(t-1)\times d_{x}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}. Concretely, we consider the model

yt\displaystyle y_{t} =f∗​(xt)+vt,∀t≥1;\displaystyle=f^{*}(x_{t})+v_{t},\quad\quad\ \ \ \ \forall t\geq 1; (1)
xt\displaystyle x_{t} =gt​(x1,…,xt−1),∀t>1.\displaystyle=g_{t}(x_{1},\dots,x_{t-1}),\quad\forall t>1. (2)

Here, x1∈ℝdxx_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} is a random vector drawn from some probability distribution 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}. Thus, Eq. 1 and Eq. 2 implicitly specify the distribution of yty_{t} (conditioned on xtx_{t}) and of xtx_{t} (conditioned on x1,…,xt−1x_{1},\dots,x_{t-1}). By defining the relationship between data of different tasks, the transformation gtg_{t} captures the dependency among these tasks (cf. Fig. 1a). While we interpret Eq. 1 and Eq. 2 as a task dependency model in the CL context, our main motivation is from the control literature: Eq. 1 and Eq. 2 define a nonlinear dynamical system where xtx_{t}’s are system states and f∗f^{*} consists of system parameters to be identified. Different from standard dynamical systems, our model has no control input and Eq. 2 is in the absence of noise. This is for the sake of simplicity, and it is not difficult to extend our results to the case of noisy task dependency where xtx_{t} is equal to gt​(x1,…,xt−1)g_{t}(x_{1},\dots,x_{t-1}) up to additive random noise. One more difference is that in Eq. 2 we require xtx_{t} to depend on all the past x1,…,xt−1x_{1},\dots,x_{t-1}, while a common special case is of the Markov type xt=gt​(xt−1)x_{t}=g_{t}(x_{t-1}). We discuss more examples and motivations in Section 2.2.

Samples and Memory. For task 11, we sample mm i.i.d. input data points {x1,i}i=1m\{x_{1,i}\}_{i=1}^{m} from distribution 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}, that is

{x1,i}i=1m​∼i.i.d.​𝒟1.\displaystyle\{x_{1,i}\}_{i=1}^{m}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{D}_{1}. (3)

We will omit the comma and write x1​ix_{1i} for x1,ix_{1,i} if it does not cause confusion. For task t>1t>1, we generate input-output pairs (xt​i,yt​ix_{ti},y_{ti}) as per Eq. 1 and Eq. 2, that is we have

xt​i=gt​(x1​i,…,xt−1,i),∀t>1,i∈[m],\displaystyle x_{ti}=g_{t}(x_{1i},\dots,x_{t-1,i}),\quad\forall t>1,i\in[m], (4)

and yt​i=f∗​(xt​i)+vt​iy_{ti}=f^{*}(x_{ti})+v_{ti} for some noise vt​iv_{ti}. Fig. 1b visualizes the input samples {xt​i}t∈[T],i∈[m]\{x_{ti}\}_{t\in[T],i\in[m]} in a matrix form.

Motivated by memory-based methods in CL, we furthermore assume the availability of only part of the samples indexed by some fixed subset ℳ\mathcal{M} of [T]×[m][T]\times[m]. That is, (xt​i,yt​i)(x_{ti},y_{ti}) is available for training if and only if (t,i)∈ℳ(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}. The available inputs (xt​i)(t,i)∈ℳ(x_{ti})_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}} can be arranged into a T×mT\times m partial matrix (cf. Fig. 1c). The tt-th row of this matrix corresponds to the stored data {(xt​i,yt​i)}i∈ℛt\{(x_{ti},y_{ti})\}_{i\in\mathcal{R}_{t}} of task tt; we index them by ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}, a subset of [m][m] (Fig. 1c). Let nt:=|ℛt|n_{t}:=|\mathcal{R}_{t}|. We have nt≤mn_{t}\leq m. We have |ℛT|=m|\mathcal{R}_{T}|=m, as we assume full access to the samples of the current task TT.

Given the above problem setup, our goal is to learn f∗f^{*} from the available samples indexed by ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Remark 1.

Constructing ℳ\mathcal{M} is to select samples to store and is an interesting CL topic. This can be done via some information-theoretical criterion or optimization (Borsos et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2022; Elenter et al., 2023). On the other hand, simple strategies such as random sampling or reservoir sampling (Vitter, 1985) actually work very well (Dokania et al., 2019; Araujo et al., 2022). We assume ℳ\mathcal{M} is fixed, while our results apply directly to the case where ℳ\mathcal{M} is constructed via random or reservoir sampling.

Comparison to Other Modeling Assumptions. To highlight the advantages of our modeling assumptions, we first consider the following alternatives:

  • •

    A common setting is that the samples within each task are i.i.d., but the samples across tasks be dependent in an arbitrary way; namely, xt​ix_{ti} depends on xτ​jx_{\tau j} for any t≠τt\neq\tau and any i,ji,j (cf. Fig. 2a). This is a practical and general setup as considered in Example 2, but it is also a challenging situation for which prior work does not shed light on the benefits of learning from multiple dependent tasks.

  • •

    In another setting, one has TT distributions {𝒟t}t∈[T]\{\mathcal{D}_{t}\}_{t\in[T]}. For each tt, one draws i.i.d. samples xt​ix_{ti} from 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. Thus, the samples of all tasks are independent, though not identically distributed (cf. Fig. 2b). This setting is intuitive but of less technical interest, as the proof of estimation error bounds is significantly simplified due to the full independence.

In comparison, our proposed setting strikes a balance by assuming that the data across tasks are dependent in a specific way (cf. Fig. 2c). While the proof is still nontrivial under our setting, the intuitive benefit is clear: it reduces the potential dependency across tasks, making it possible to derive better bounds (Fig. 2a versus Fig. 2c).

Comparison to Task Dependency Assumptions. Learning from the full data (or partial data) as shown in Fig. 1 can be viewed as a multitask learning problem where each task tt has mm (or ntn_{t}) samples (Maurer et al., 2016; Tripuraneni et al., 2020; Tripuraneni et al., 2021; Du et al., 2021). The differences from recent multitask learning papers are twofold: Our samples across tasks are dependent, as specified in Eq. 2; our definition of task dependency is different. In fact, pursuing a suitable definition of task dependency has led to fruitful developments in multitask learning and transfer learning. Ben-David and Borbely (2008) capture the notion of task dependency by an equivalence relation between functions in the hypothesis space. This allows empirical risk minimization to be conducted in a smaller (quotient) space, which translates to a tighter theoretical bound. But this benefit is compromised as optimization over such a space is difficult. A practical task dependency assumption, as considered by Maurer et al. (2016); Tripuraneni et al. (2020); Tripuraneni et al. (2021); Du et al. (2021) and even in earlier work (Caruana, 1997; Baxter, 2000; Argyriou et al., 2006), posits that each task tt admits a predictor of the form ft∘ϕf_{t}\circ\phi, where ϕ\phi is called the shared representation and ftf_{t} a task-specific predictor often assumed to be linear. Applications of this setting include deep networks with a shared backbone representing ϕ\phi and multiple task-specific heads representing ftf_{t}. However, such a network needs knowledge of the task corresponding to an input in order to select the corresponding head, which makes it inapplicable to some CL scenarios where no such task identity is available at test time (e.g., class-incremental or domain-incremental learning) (van de Ven et al., 2022; Ramesh and Chaudhari, 2022).

2.2 Motivation and Context

We now discuss several lines of prior work that motivate our problem settings and task dependency assumptions.

CL Context. Our nonlinear transformation gtg_{t} in Eq. 2 covers as special cases the rotations or permutations that arise in CL datasets known respectively as rotated MNIST and permuted MNIST, where task 11 is to classify the MNIST images x1x_{1}, and the images xtx_{t} of subsequent tasks are obtained by rotating or permuting the pixels of x1x_{1}. While these datasets appear artificial, they have been used to benchmark many CL methods, which make themselves practically significant. The task dependency with rotations was theoretically analyzed recently by Goldfarb and Hand (2023); Goldfarb et al. (2024) in the case of two linear regression tasks. In these works, the rotation acts only on the input data and does not change the labels, similarly to the setting of Ben-David and Borbely (2008).

Motivation from Machine Learning and Control. Note that gtg_{t} defines a type of autoregressive models which have played major roles in machine learning for computing with sequential data (Bishop, 2006, Chapter 13). Classic such models include (hidden) Markov models and linear dynamical systems, and they find ample applications in speech recognition, language modeling, and control systems where gtg_{t} is often to be learned. Furthermore, recent empirical research shows that deep generative models such as diffusion models can transform one distribution or dataset into another. In diffusion models the transformation between consecutive time steps is of the type identity-plus-noise. Different from our deterministic gtg_{t}, this is a random transformation due to the use of random noise.

Our data generation protocol Eq. 1 and Eq. 2 also find motivations in recent research on learning from many trajectories or dependent data (Tu et al., 2024; Ziemann et al., 2023; Ziemann and Tu, 2022; Tadipatri et al., 2025). A major difference is that these works assume the availability of full data (Fig. 1b). Instead, we are motivated by CL scenarios (memory-based methods), and consider a more general situation of learning from many incomplete or partial trajectories (Fig. 1c). At a technical level, we build upon the proof ideas of Ziemann et al. (2023); Tadipatri et al. (2025) but also make extensions for cases such as partial trajectories, weighted objectives, data-dependent regularization, and data-dependent weights (cf. Section 3).

Geometric Vision Context. In geometric vision (Hartley and Zisserman, 2004), gtg_{t} also arises. There, a classical scenario is point cloud registration (Arun et al., 1987): Given two point clouds {x1​i}i∈[m]\{x_{1i}\}_{i\in[m]} and {x2​i}i∈[m]\{x_{2i}\}_{i\in[m]} of the same scene captured by a moving camera, the goal is to find some Euclidean transformation g2g_{2} that aligns them; ideally we have x2​i=g2​(x1​i)x_{2i}=g_{2}(x_{1i}) for all i∈[m]i\in[m], while it is possible that not all points of the scene are captured and some points are missing (cf. Fig. 1c). Here, g2g_{2} models how the camera moves and is independent of the point clouds. Finally, a sequence of multiple point clouds arise naturally, as the camera moves and continually measures the scene.

3 Theoretical Contributions

We first describe the notations and technical assumptions (Section 3.1). Then we introduce our theory for weighted experience replay with regularization (Section 3.2), data-dependent regularization (Section 3.3), and data-dependent weights (Section 3.4).

There is a sufficiently large number rxr_{x} such that for every f,f′∈ℱf,f^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F} the following hold with KG=𝒪~​(𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(rx))K_{G}=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}({\mathsf{poly}}(r_{x})):

supz∈𝔹rx​(dx)‖Gf,t​(z)−Gf′,t​(z)‖2≤KG⋅‖f−f′‖ℱ;\displaystyle\sup_{z\in\mathbb{B}_{r_{x}}(d_{x})}\|G_{f,t}(z)-G_{f^{\prime},t}(z)\|_{2}\leq K_{G}\cdot\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}};
supz∈𝔹rx​(dx)|‖Gf,t​(z)‖22−‖Gf′,t​(z)‖22|≤KG​‖f−f′‖ℱ.\displaystyle\sup_{z\in\mathbb{B}_{r_{x}}(d_{x})}\left|\|G_{f,t}(z)\|_{2}^{2}-\|G_{f^{\prime},t}(z)\|_{2}^{2}\right|\leq K_{G}\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}.

Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 are standard. Assumption 4 imposes Lipschitz-type conditions on our parameterized function fθf_{\theta} and direct difference map Gf,tG_{f,t} and it requires rxr_{x} to be sufficiently large; we will show the precise values of rxr_{x} in the full version of our theorems in the appendix. Roughly speaking, Eq. 6 holds for deep networks with bounded parameters and bounded inputs, while the rest inequalities hold true as soon as all ff and gtg_{t}’s are Lipschitz continuous. Note that rotations and permutations aforementioned are Lipschitz continuous.

3.2 Recovery Guarantee 1: Weighted Replay With Data-Independent Regularization

In this and next two sections, we introduce our main theorems (see Table 2 for a summary).

Inspired by memory-based and regularization-based methods, we formulate the following problem:

minθ∈Θ⁡1T​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt⋅ℒ⁡(yt​i,fθ​(xt​i))+λ⋅ΩT​(θ).\displaystyle\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\cdot\mathcal{L}\Big(y_{ti},f_{\theta}(x_{ti})\Big)+\lambda\cdot\Omega_{T}(\theta). (7)

In Eq. 7, we use the squared loss ℒ⁡(y,y^)=‖y^−y‖22\mathcal{L}(y,\hat{y})=\|\hat{y}-y\|_{2}^{2}, as it is empirically useful in CL practice (McDonnell et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2025) and is a common objective of interest in CL theory. The factor 1/nt1/n_{t} normalizes the loss of each task. Each wtw_{t} is some non-negative weight for task tt, and we assume wT>0w_{T}>0, as we have full data for the current task TT. Moreover, we assume that wtw_{t}’s are hyperparameters, chosen by a user and independent of data. The function ΩT​(⋅)\Omega_{T}(\cdot) serves the purpose of regularization, and it is weighted by some non-negative number λ\lambda. Thus, Eq. 7 amounts to minimizing a multitask loss with regularization ΩT​(⋅)\Omega_{T}(\cdot). The generality of Eq. 7 stems from its flexibility to choose weights wtw_{t} and regularization ΩT​(⋅)\Omega_{T}(\cdot). For example, experience replay or rehearsal amounts to solving Eq. 7 with λ=0\lambda=0, while regularization-based methods often set wT=1w_{T}=1 and set all previous weights to 00. Here, we assume ΩT​(θ)\Omega_{T}(\theta) is independent of data and noise, as is often the case in machine learning (Goodfellow et al., 2016, Chapter 7), and as considered in some CL algorithms (Kumar et al., 2025; Lewandowski et al., 2025). For our results on data-dependent regularizers, see Section 3.3.

Remark 2.

To unify memory-based and regularization-based methods, Wang et al. (2024) considers a general formulation similar to Eq. 7. Wang et al. (2024) has a specific algorithmic focus and its formulation is not leveraged in full generality for theoretical developments, while we develop statistical recovery results for Eq. 7 and its variants.

We are ready to state our main result of this section:

Theorem 1.

Fix δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). Suppose Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 3 hold. Recall that noise vtv_{t} is conditionally sub-Gaussian with proxy variance ν2\nu^{2}. Let θ^T∈Θ⊂ℝp\hat{\theta}_{T}\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{p} be a global minimizer of Eq. 7 with regularization parameter λ\lambda satisfying λ≲1T​maxt∈[T]​wtnt\lambda\lesssim\frac{1}{T}\max_{t\in[T]}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}. Define

κ:=supf∈ℱ\{f∗}supt∈[T],wt>0𝔼​[‖Gf,t​(x1)‖24]1/2𝔼⁡[‖Gf,t​(x1)‖22].\displaystyle\kappa:=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}\ \backslash\{f^{*}\}}\sup_{t\in[T],w_{t}>0}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\|G_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{4}\right]^{1/2}}{\mathbb{E}\left[\|G_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]}. (8)

Assume nt≥κ2⋅𝒪~​(p​ln⁡(T)+ln⁡(1/δ))n_{t}\geq\kappa^{2}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(p\ln(T)+\ln(1/\delta)\right) for all t∈[T]t\in[T]. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta the weighted estimation error 1T​∑t∈[T]wt⋅𝔼​‖f∗​(xt)−fθ^T​(xt)‖22\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}w_{t}\cdot\mathbb{E}\|f^{*}(x_{t})-f_{\hat{\theta}_{T}}(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2} is bounded above by

𝒪~​(ν2​(p+ln⁡(1/δ))+𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(σ)T⋅maxt∈[T]⁡wtnt).\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\nu^{2}(p+\ln(1/\delta))+{\mathsf{poly}}(\sigma)}{T}\cdot\max_{t\in[T]}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\right). (9)

Theorem 1 is a finite sample guarantee with bound Eq. 9 depending on variances of data (𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(σ){\mathsf{poly}}(\sigma)) and noise (ν2\nu^{2}), the number of tasks TT, the number of of available samples ntn_{t} and weight wtw_{t} of task tt (note that the bounds hides dependency on the dimensions dx,dyd_{x},d_{y} among other terms). We discuss these quantities next.

Proxy Variance of Data. Since both xi​tx_{it}’s and vi​tv_{it}’s are random, the estimation error depends on their proxy variances σ2\sigma^{2} and ν2\nu^{2}. First, the dependency on σ\sigma is 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(σ){\mathsf{poly}}(\sigma), which is because Assumption 4 introduces a polynomial dependency of rxr_{x} whose precise values depend on σ\sigma.

Weights and Sample Complexity. While prior work sets uniform weights w1=⋯=wT>0w_{1}=\cdots=w_{T}>0 to derive statistical bounds in their CL settings (Lin et al., 2023; Friedman and Meir, 2024), we prove our bound in Eq. 9 with arbitrary non-negative weights wtw_{t} (independent of data). This allows us to set different weights and acquire different theoretical insights. For example, if we set all weights but wtw_{t} to 00, then Eq. 9 becomes a single-task bound

𝔼​‖f∗​(xt)−fθ^T​(xt)‖22≤{𝒪~​(1m)T=t,𝒪~​(1nt)T>t.\mathbb{E}\|f^{*}(x_{t})-f_{\hat{\theta}_{T}}(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\leq\begin{cases}\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\frac{1}{m}\big)&T=t,\\ \tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\big)&T>t.\end{cases}

The case T=tT=t holds as we have mm samples at task tt. We now see that when transiting from task tt to task t+1t+1, forgetting occurs as the bound transits from 𝒪~​(1/m)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/m) to 𝒪~​(1/nt)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/n_{t}). However, starting from task t+1t+1, the bound remains the same, thus no significant forgetting is furthermore entailed.

If we set w1=⋯=wT>0w_{1}=\cdots=w_{T}>0, then Theorem 1 upper bounds the average error 1T​∑t∈[T]𝔼​‖f∗​(xt)−fθ^T​(xt)‖22\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\|f^{*}(x_{t})-f_{\hat{\theta}_{T}}(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2} by 𝒪~​(1T⋅mint∈[T]⁡nt)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{1}{T\cdot\min_{t\in[T]}n_{t}}\right). For this bound to be informative, we need a balanced memory that stores approximately the same number of samples for each task, which is indeed the case when we construct the memory by random sampling or reservoir sampling (Remark 1). Furthermore, this is in agreement with common CL practice, where balanced memory tends to perform better than the imbalanced ones (Dokania et al., 2019; Prabhu et al., 2020; Araujo et al., 2022). Then, given balanced memory and as TT increases, our result gets better, partly because the upper bound decreases, and partly because it provides bounds on the average error of more tasks. Finally, we note that, with non-uniform weights wt=T​ntn1+⋯+nTw_{t}=\frac{Tn_{t}}{n_{1}+\cdots+n_{T}} that sum to 11, Theorem 1 gives the bound 𝒪~​(1n1+⋯+nT)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}+\cdots+n_{T}}\right), which is with the optimal sample complexity 𝒪~​(1/(n1+⋯+nT))\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/(n_{1}+\cdots+n_{T})).

Are the above bounds too good to be true? Indeed, we have at most mm samples starting (the samples of all tasks are deterministic transformations of the mm samples from task 11); at first glance one might conclude that the sample complexity lower bound would be 𝒪~​(1/m)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/m), but Theorem 1 gives a tighter result. This is not a contradiction, the reason being that Theorem 1 assumes sufficiently many samples with m≥nt≥κ2⋅𝒪~​(p​ln⁡(T)+ln⁡(1/δ))m\geq n_{t}\geq\kappa^{2}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(p\ln(T)+\ln(1/\delta)\right), all tasks share a common predictor f∗f^{*}, and we consider the regression formulation. For example, if f∗f^{*} is linear, then with m≥pm\geq p linearly independent (random) samples the regression problem has a unique global minimizer f∗f^{*}. In this case, we can recover the true f∗f^{*} exactly, which gives us the zero bound instead of 𝒪~​(1/m)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/m).

Condition on Sufficiently Many Samples. Theorem 1 assumes nt≥κ2⋅𝒪~​(p​ln⁡(T)+ln⁡(1/δ))n_{t}\geq\kappa^{2}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(p\ln(T)+\ln(1/\delta)\right), that is, every task stores sufficiently many samples. To understand what this assumption imposes, it suffices to analyze the role of κ\kappa. While computing the numerical values of κ\kappa is difficult, from Assumption 3 we know κ\kappa is finite. More can be said if we make extra assumptions on how tasks are dependent (note that κ\kappa depends on Gf,tG_{f,t} and Gf,tG_{f,t} encodes the information about task dependency):

Example 3.

Assume the function class ℱ\mathcal{F} consists of linear functions and all entries of x1x_{1} are i.i.d. Gaussian, sampled from 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). Consider two tasks with g2:x1↦1010​x1g_{2}:x_{1}\mapsto 10^{10}x_{1}. With two functions f,f∗∈ℱf,f^{*}\in\mathcal{F} fixed and parameterized by θ,θ∗\theta,\theta^{*}, respectively, we have Gf,t​(x1)=(θ−θ∗)⊤​x1G_{f,t}(x_{1})=(\theta-\theta^{*})^{\top}x_{1}. Since Gf,t​(x1)G_{f,t}(x_{1}) is also a zero-mean Gaussian, a standard calculation of its fourth and second moments gives κ2=3\kappa^{2}=3. Note that the scaling factor 101010^{10} has no effect in κ\kappa.

We have κ2≤3\kappa^{2}\leq 3 if Gaussianity of Example 3 is replaced with strict sub-Gaussianity. Finally, we note that κ\kappa is upper bounded by some universal constant for sub-Gaussian data.

Robustness to Distant Distributions. Example 3 generalizes to multiple tasks with gtg_{t}’s being of the form x1↦st​xtx_{1}\mapsto s_{t}x_{t} for some sts_{t}. Such a simple example of gtg_{t}’s can in fact make a difficult case for analysis. Indeed, it affects the Lipschitz parameter LGL_{G} and radius rxr_{x} in Assumption 4. That said, all of our bounds exhibit only a logarithmic dependency on LGL_{G}, rxr_{x}, so our theorems allow sts_{t} to be a polynomial function of problem parameters. The second difficulty Example 3 brings manifests itself, not in our theorem, but in prior work. Indeed, for large sts_{t}, the data distributions of two tasks, 𝒩⁡(0,Idx)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d_{x}}) and 𝒩⁡(0,st2​Idx)\mathcal{N}(0,s_{t}^{2}I_{d_{x}}), could be very distant; here IdxI_{d_{x}} is the dx×dxd_{x}\times d_{x} identity matrix. This distance has fundamental impacts on many statistical bounds that depend linearly on this distance:

Remark 3.

The theory of Mansour et al. (2009) on domain adaptation bounds statistical errors of the second task (i.e., target task) by the discrepancy distance between distributions π1,π2\pi_{1},\pi_{2} of the first task (source task) and the second task. The discrepancy dist⁡(π1,π2)\dist(\pi_{1},\pi_{2}), defined as

supθ1,θ2∈Θ|𝔼π1​ℒ​(fθ1​(z),fθ2​(z))−𝔼π2​ℒ​(fθ1​(z),fθ2​(z))|,\sup_{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\in\Theta}\left|\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{1}}\mathcal{L}\left(f_{\theta_{1}}(z),f_{\theta_{2}}(z)\right)-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{2}}\mathcal{L}\left(f_{\theta_{1}}(z),f_{\theta_{2}}(z)\right)\right|,

measures the similarities between π1,π2\pi_{1},\pi_{2}. If dist⁡(π1,π2)\dist(\pi_{1},\pi_{2}) is small, we might expect some benefits of learning task 1 prior to task 2 (e.g., small errors on task 2). This basic intuition is extended to various settings, including online multitask learning, transfer learning, and continual learning (Mohri and Muñoz Medina, 2012; Wang et al., 2023; Ye and Bors, 2022). That said, the discrepancy can be large in Example 3 with the squared loss ℒ⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathcal{L}(\cdot,\cdot). Indeed, set π1=𝒩⁡(0,Idx)\pi_{1}=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d_{x}}) and π2=𝒩⁡(0,s2​Idx)\pi_{2}=\mathcal{N}(0,s^{2}I_{d_{x}}) with s≫1s\gg 1, andone verifies dist⁡(π1,π2)=(s2−1)⋅diam⁡(Θ)2\dist(\pi_{1},\pi_{2})=(s^{2}-1)\cdot\diam(\Theta)^{2}, that is, the distance grows unbounded as ss increases; their corresponding bound is vacuous in this scenario. In consequence, the proof based on such a discrepancy is unable to handle simple yet distant tasks. For a similar reason, the recent PAC-Bayes bound of Friedman and Meir (2024) easily becomes vacuous due to the presence of a similar discrepancy term.

Our final note on Theorem 1 is a comparison to the experience replay theory of Peng et al. (2023a).

Remark 4.

Theorem 3 of Peng et al. (2023a) provides the bound 𝒪~​(1nt)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{1}{n_{t}}) on the excess risk of Eq. 7 with λ=0\lambda=0 for each task tt. This directly implies the bound 𝒪~​(log⁡TT​∑t∈[T]1nt)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{\log T}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}\frac{1}{n_{t}}) for the average joint loss. This bound becomes 𝒪~​(log⁡T/nt)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log T/n_{t}) when all ntn_{t}’s are of the same order. In contrast, we directly work with the average estimation error, and our bound has an 𝒪~​(1/T)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T) dependency on TT.

3.3 Recovery Guarantee 2: Data-Dependent Regularization and Knowledge Distillation

Theorem 1 in Section 3.2 assumes the regularizer is independent of data. On the other hand, it is not uncommon to utilize data-dependent regularizers for CL. A typical data-dependent regularizer used in CL is knowledge distillation, that is to match the (intermediate) outputs of the current network fθf_{\theta} and the previously learned network fθ^tf_{\hat{\theta}_{t}} at stored samples. This motivates the following CL method:

  • •

    (Step 1) Set hyperparameter βT>0\beta_{T}>0. Then solve

    θ^T∈argminθ∈ΘβT​∑i∈[m]ℒ⁡(yT​i,fθ​(xT​i))+ΩT​(θ),\displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{T}\in\mathop{\rm argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\beta_{T}\sum_{i\in[m]}\mathcal{L}\Big(y_{Ti},f_{\theta}(x_{Ti})\Big)+\Omega_{T}(\theta), (10)

    where ΩT​(⋅)\Omega_{T}(\cdot) is either of the following two regularizers:

    ΩT​(θ)\displaystyle\Omega_{T}(\theta) =∑t∈[T−1]∑i∈ℛtβt⋅‖fθ​(xt​i)−fθ^T−1​(xt​i)‖22\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in[T-1]}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}\beta_{t}\cdot\|f_{\theta}(x_{ti})-f_{\hat{\theta}_{T-1}}(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2} (11)
    ΩT​(θ)\displaystyle\Omega_{T}(\theta) =∑t∈[T−1]∑i∈ℛtβt⋅‖fθ​(xt​i)−fθ^t​(xt​i)‖22\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in[T-1]}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}\beta_{t}\cdot\|f_{\theta}(x_{ti})-f_{\hat{\theta}_{t}}(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2} (12)
  • •

    (Step 2) Choose indices ℛT⊂[m]\mathcal{R}_{T}\subset[m]. Store {(xT​i,yT​i)}i∈ℛT\{(x_{Ti},y_{Ti})\}_{i\in\mathcal{R}_{T}}. Increase TT. Go back to Step 1.

The above method are with regularizer Eq. 11 or Eq. 12 to compute θ^1,…,θ^T\hat{\theta}_{1},\dots,\hat{\theta}_{T} continually. Regularizer Eq. 11 aims to match fθf_{\theta} and fθ^T−1f_{\hat{\theta}_{T-1}} on all previous tasks, while regularizer Eq. 12 aims to match fθf_{\theta} and fθ^tf_{\hat{\theta}_{t}} on each task tt (∀t∈[T−1]\forall t\in[T-1]). In both cases, it is understood that task 11 is solved without regularization and that the algorithm consistently chooses either Eq. 11 or Eq. 12. Computationally, for Eq. 12 we can store fθ^t​(xt​i)f_{\hat{\theta}_{t}}(x_{ti}) after training task tt, while for Eq. 11 we need to compute fθ^T−1​(xt​i)f_{\hat{\theta}_{T-1}}(x_{ti}) after training task T−1T-1. For both regularizers, we have the following theorem.

Theorem 2.

Fix δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). Let κ\kappa be as in Eq. 8. Suppose Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 3 hold. Recall that noise vtv_{t} is conditionally sub-Gaussian with proxy variance ν2\nu^{2}. Assume nt≥κ2⋅𝒪~​(p​ln⁡(T)+ln⁡(1/δ))n_{t}\geq\kappa^{2}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(p\ln(T)+\ln(1/\delta)\right) for all t∈[T]t\in[T]. If θ^1,…,θ^T∈Θ⊂ℝp\hat{\theta}_{1},\dots,\hat{\theta}_{T}\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{p} are global minimizers of Eq. 11 with βt=1/4T−t\beta_{t}=1/4^{T-t}. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta the weighted error ∑t∈[T]βt​nt∑t∈[T]βt​nt⋅𝔼​‖f∗​(xt)−fθ^T​(xt)‖22\sum_{t\in[T]}\frac{\beta_{t}n_{t}}{\sum_{t\in[T]}\beta_{t}n_{t}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\|f^{*}(x_{t})-f_{\hat{\theta}_{T}}(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2} is bounded above by

𝒪~​(ν2​(p​T+ln⁡(1/δ))+𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(σ)∑t∈[T]βt​nt).\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\nu^{2}(pT+\ln(1/\delta))+{\mathsf{poly}}(\sigma)}{\sum_{t\in[T]}\beta_{t}n_{t}}\right). (13)

If θ^1,…,θ^T\hat{\theta}_{1},\dots,\hat{\theta}_{T} are solutions to Eq. 12, then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta we have Eq. 13 holds as well.

In Theorem 2, the error term that we bound has its weights on distances ‖f∗​(xt)−fθ^T​(xt)‖22\|f^{*}(x_{t})-f_{\hat{\theta}_{T}}(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2} decay exponentially as tt decreases, meaning that Eq. 13 carries exponentially less control over the distances on past tasks. Therefore, Theorem 2 is informative for a small number of the most recent tasks, and to some extent, it illuminates the limits of regularization-based methods in combating forgetting. In fact, this bound is worse than that of Theorem 1 for experience replay. This aligns with empirical observations that experience replay typically outperforms regularization-based approaches; for example, see Table 4 of (Prabhu et al., 2020), which compares LwF (Li and Hoiem, 2017) and GDumb (Prabhu et al., 2020).

On a technical note, bound Eq. 13 itself could be sub-optimal for two reasons. First, since the algorithm analyzed involves all predictors fθ^1,…,fθ^Tf_{\hat{\theta}_{1}},\dots,f_{\hat{\theta}_{T}}, all of which depend on data, we have to run an ε\varepsilon-net argument on the product space ΘT\Theta^{T} in ℝp​T\mathbb{R}^{pT}, which brings the dependency p​TpT. Second, the exponential forgetting phenomenon is due to our choice βt=1/4T−t\beta_{t}=1/4^{T-t}. This choice is crucial, as it prevents the bound from getting exponentially large. Improving Theorem 2 in these aspects is left for future work.

We finish the section by remarking on existing theoretical contributions on regularization-based methods:

Remark 5.

The analysis of Heckel (2022); Li et al. (2023); Zhao et al. (2024); Levinstein et al. (2025) relies on linear models or the kernel regime. The analysis of Zhu et al. (2025) relies on either the assumption of shared global minimizers or a noisy linear regression model. The setting of Yin et al. (2020) is general, but the error bound of their Theorem 4 contains the distance of the form ‖θ^T−θ^t‖2\|\hat{\theta}_{T}-\hat{\theta}_{t}\|_{2}. This is a random variable whose dependency on problem parameters is unclear. In contrast, our bound in Eq. 13 contains only parameters related to the problem configuration. We achieve this via several key inequalities that give rise to a recurrence relation, which we unroll to eliminate all random variables related to θ^t\hat{\theta}_{t}.

3.4 Recovery Guarantee 3: Data-Dependent Weights and Constrained Optimization

Our formulation Eq. 7 in Section 3.2 assumes the weights are independent of data. Here, we consider

θ^T∈argminθ∈Θ1T​∑(t,i)∈ℳw~tnt⋅ℒ⁡(yt​i,fθ​(xt​i)),\displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{T}\in\mathop{\rm argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{\tilde{w}_{t}}{n_{t}}\cdot\mathcal{L}\Big(y_{ti},f_{\theta}(x_{ti})\Big), (14)

where weight w~t\tilde{w}_{t} is a random variable depending on all data and noise. While we allowed zero weights in Section 3.2 to study regularization-based methods without replay, here we assume w~t≠0\tilde{w}_{t}\neq 0 (∀t∈[T]\forall t\in[T]), or otherwise formulation Eq. 14 reduces to a case with fewer tasks. Then, dividing the smallest weight if necessary, we assume w~t∈[1,W]\tilde{w}_{t}\in[1,W].

There are multiple ways to choose w^t\hat{w}_{t} in a data-dependent fashion. For example, set w^t\hat{w}_{t} to be proportional (or inversely proportional) to the loss of task tt (in light of boosting (Schapire, 1990; Ramesh and Chaudhari, 2022; Wang et al., 2023) or iteratively reweighted least-squares (Daubechies et al., 2010; Kümmerle et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2023b)), or solve a bilevel program in weight variables that represent coresets (Borsos et al., 2020), or set the weights to the values of dual variables which arise in primal-dual methods for constrained learning (Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017; Chamon et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2023a; Elenter et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

We now give recovery guarantees for Eq. 14:

Theorem 3.

Fix δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). Let κ\kappa be as in Eq. 8. Suppose Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 3 hold. Recall that noise vtv_{t} is conditionally sub-Gaussian with proxy variance ν2\nu^{2} and that w~t∈[1,W]\tilde{w}_{t}\in[1,W]. Let θ^T∈Θ⊂ℝp\hat{\theta}_{T}\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{p} be a global minimizer of Eq. 14. Assume nt≥κ2⋅𝒪~​(p​ln⁡(T)+ln⁡(1/δ))n_{t}\geq\kappa^{2}\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(p\ln(T)+\ln(1/\delta)\right) for all t∈[T]t\in[T] and W≤1+1T​ntW\leq 1+\frac{1}{Tn_{t}}. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the average estimation error 1T​∑t∈[T]𝔼​‖f∗​(xt)−fθ^T​(xt)‖22\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\|f^{*}(x_{t})-f_{\hat{\theta}_{T}}(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2} is bounded above by

𝒪~​(ν2​(p+ln⁡(1/δ))+max⁡{𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(σ),ln⁡(σ​T)}T​mint∈[T]​nt).\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\nu^{2}(p+\ln(1/\delta))+\max\{{\mathsf{poly}}(\sigma),\ln(\sigma T)\}}{T\min_{t\in[T]}n_{t}}\right). (15)

The bound of Theorem 3 follows from that of Theorem 1, and in fact they are identical except assumption W≤1+1T​ntW\leq 1+\frac{1}{Tn_{t}}. This extra condition is what we pay for the case of data-dependent weights. Due to a number of differences in the settings, Theorem 3 is not directly comparable to theoretical results of Li et al. (2024); Peng et al. (2023a); Chamon et al. (2022). However, a distinguishing aspect is that, as TT gets large, our bound would in general get better, while their bounds deteriorate. This is because we explicitly model the dependency between tasks and take advantage of it in the proofs, while their proofs do not consider task dependency and need instead to apply TT concentration inequalities, one for each task (Example 2).

4 Conclusion

Inspired by nonlinear dynamical systems and several other topics, we formalized a notion of task dependency for continual learning of nonlinear regression tasks. Building upon it, we developed some recovery guarantees for commonly used CL methods that involve replay, regularization (e.g., knowledge distillation), and data-dependent weighting. The estimation error bounds we derived are well-behaved, as they diminish as the number of samples tends to infinity or for sufficiently small noise. The key to proving our theorems is a careful balance we maintain between the generality of the problem formulation and the tightness of the resulting bounds; put differently, this can also be viewed as a limitation: our proof framework does not support deriving stronger guarantees for more general scenarios where different tasks are dependent arbitrarily (Fig. 2). The other limitation is this: Our results are based on the assumption that the number of stored samples per task exceeds the dimension of the parameter space. It will be of interest to relax this assumption and furthermore extend our results to the overparameterized regime.

In the future, we plan to improve the bounds for regularization-based methods (Theorem 2) by exploring more specific settings such as linear models (cf. Remark 5), to extend our Theorem 3 with data-dependent weights within the constrained learning framework of Chamon et al. (2022) that guarantees the feasibility of constraints, and to extend the insights of the paper here for other CL paradigms (e.g., expansion-based methods). Also, note that our analysis is independent of the algorithmic choice, and in the future we plan to analyze the effect of the algorithm on the recovery errors as well.

Recovery Guarantees for Continual Learning of Dependent Tasks: Memory, Data-Dependent Regularization, and Data-Dependent Weights:
Supplementary Materials

 

In this material, we will present proofs of results, examples, related work, extra discussion on extensions, and preliminaries for the main draft. The below is the table of contents of this material:

Contents

Appendix A Extra Details on Main Paper

A.1 Extra Notations and Figures

In our proof, we will need to index our data by columns, thus we extend Fig. 1 and include examples of the index sets ℳi⊂[T]\mathcal{M}_{i}\subset[T] for each column ii. Specifically, the ii-th column of this partial matrix in Fig. 3c corresponds to a partial trajectory of samples {(xt​i,yt​i)}t∈ℳi\{(x_{ti},y_{ti})\}_{t\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}.

A.2 On Task-Specific Predictors

At first glance, Eq. 1 seems to ask all tasks to share a common true predictor f∗f^{*}, similarly to prior work (Evron et al., 2022; Peng and Risteski, 2022; Peng et al., 2023a; Li et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Elenter et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025). But the extra presence of Eq. 2 on top of Eq. 1 recovers a case where each task tt possesses its own predictor ft∗f_{t}^{*}:

Example 4.

Consider the following model:

yt=ft∗(x¯t)+vt,x¯t=g¯t(x¯1,…,x¯t−1),ft∗=ft−1∗∘ht.\begin{split}y_{t}&=f_{t}^{*}(\overline{x}_{t})+v_{t},\ \ \overline{x}_{t}=\overline{g}_{t}(\overline{x}_{1},\dots,\overline{x}_{t-1}),\\ f_{t}^{*}&=f_{t-1}^{*}\circ h_{t}.\end{split} (16)

In Eq. 16, the first two equations are identical to Eq. 1 and Eq. 2, despite the different notations x¯t\overline{x}_{t} and g¯t\overline{g}_{t}. Moreover, Eq. 16 contains an extra equation ft∗=ft−1∗∘htf_{t}^{*}=f_{t-1}^{*}\circ h_{t}, where hth_{t} is some known invertible mapping capturing a relationship between the predictors of two consecutive tasks. Let h1h_{1} be the identity mapping, and write h1:t:=h1∘⋯∘hth_{1:t}:=h_{1}\circ\cdots\circ h_{t} and xt:=h1:t(x¯t)x_{t}:=h_{1:t}(\overline{x}_{t}). By basic algebra we eliminate the presence of ft∗,x¯tf_{t}^{*},\overline{x}_{t} in Eq. 16, and obtain yt=f1∗​(xt)+vty_{t}=f_{1}^{*}(x_{t})+v_{t} and xt=h1:t(g¯t(h1−1(x1),…,h1:t−1−1(xt−1)))x_{t}=h_{1:t}(\overline{g}_{t}(h_{1}^{-1}(x_{1}),\dots,h_{1:t-1}^{-1}(x_{t-1}))). The former equation is identical to Eq. 1 with f∗=f1∗f^{*}=f_{1}^{*}, and the latter equation on xtx_{t} defines gtg_{t} in Eq. 2. Thus, estimating f1∗f_{1}^{*} in Eq. 16 reduces to estimating f∗f^{*} in Eq. 1 and Eq. 2 with a particular choice of gtg_{t}. Moreover, once f1∗f_{1}^{*} is estimated, we estimate all other ftf_{t}’s via ft∗=ft−1∗∘htf_{t}^{*}=f_{t-1}^{*}\circ h_{t}. Conversely, our model reduces to Eq. 16 when hth_{t}’s are all identity mappings. Thus, when hth_{t} is known and invertible, imposing task dependency on predictors Eq. 16 is equivalent to imposing such dependency on input samples Eq. 2.

Remark 6.

Consider two tasks with linear predictors f1∗,f2∗f_{1}^{*},f_{2}^{*} parameterized by θ1∗,θ2∗\theta_{1}^{*},\theta_{2}^{*} respectively, and assume they are related by some invertible matrix H2H_{2}, that is θ2∗=H2​θ1∗\theta_{2}^{*}=H_{2}\theta_{1}^{*}. Since such H2H_{2} always exists, if H2H_{2} is unknown, then the relationship θ2∗=H2​θ1∗\theta_{2}^{*}=H_{2}\theta_{1}^{*} gives us no extra information for learning either θ1∗\theta_{1}^{*} or θ2∗\theta_{2}^{*}. Thus, to understand the benefit of having θ2∗=H2​θ1∗\theta_{2}^{*}=H_{2}\theta_{1}^{*}, we consider H2H_{2} is known. Furthermore, in Peng and Vidal (2025); Dar et al. (2024), the relationship θ2∗=H2​θ1∗\theta_{2}^{*}=H_{2}\theta_{1}^{*} is assumed to hold up to some additive Gaussian noise. In Peng and Vidal (2025), it is shown that Kalman filtering and smoothing improve the performance on task 1 after learning task 2, an example of positive backward transfer. In Dar et al. (2024), a transfer learning setup is considered, and it is shown that learning task 1 would benefit learning task 2 in the underparameterized case but might hurt otherwise (Dar et al., 2024, Fig. 1).

A.3 On Assumption 4

We claimed in the main paper that Assumption 4 holds true as soon as all ff and gtg_{t}’s are Lipschitz continuous. A more precise statement of it is shown below in Lemma 1.

Lemma 1.

Suppose that each transformation gig_{i} is Lipschitz continuous with constant Lg,i​(i∈[T])L_{g,i}\;(i\!\in[T]). Assume ℱ\mathcal{F} consist of functions f:ℝdx→ℝdyf:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} such that f⁡(z)<∞f(z)<\infty for any finite input zz. Consider the ball 𝔹r′​(dx)\mathbb{B}_{r^{\prime}}(d_{x}) of radius r′:=r⋅max⁡∏i=1tt∈[T]⁡Lg,ir^{\prime}:=r\cdot\max_{t\in[T]}\prod_{i=1}^{t}L_{g,i}. Suppose Assumption 2 and Eq. 6 hold with Lipschitz parameter LℱL_{\mathcal{F}} and with the following norm ∥⋅∥ℱ\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{F}}:

‖f‖ℱ:=supz∈𝔹r′​(dx)‖f⁡(z)‖2.\displaystyle\|f\|_{\mathcal{F}}:=\sup_{z\in\mathbb{B}_{r^{\prime}}(d_{x})}\|f(z)\|_{2}.

Furthermore, assume ff is Lipschitz continuous with respect to its input with also constant LℱL_{\mathcal{F}}. Then rest conditions in Assumption 4 hold with

LG=2​Lℱ​max⁡∏i=1tt∈[T]⁡Lg,i,KG=max⁡(1,2​r​LG+2​Cmax).\displaystyle L_{G}=2L_{\mathcal{F}}\max_{t\in[T]}\prod_{i=1}^{t}L_{g,i},\quad\quad K_{G}=\max\left(1,2rL_{G}+2C_{\max}\right).
Proof.

First note that we have (for all z,z′∈ℝdxz,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}, for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, and for all t∈[T]t\in[T])

‖Gf,t​(z)−Gf,t​(z′)‖2=∥(f−f∗)∘gt∘⋯∘g1(z)−(f−f∗)∘gt∘⋯∘g1(z′)∥2≤2Lℱ⋅∥gt∘⋯∘g1(z)−gt∘⋯∘g1(z′)∥2≤2LℱLg,1⋅∥gt−1∘⋯∘g1(z)−gt−1∘⋯∘g1(z′)∥2≤2​Lℱ​∏i=1tLg,i⋅‖z−z′‖2.\begin{split}\|G_{f,t}(z)-G_{f,t}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}&=\|(f-f^{*})\circ g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z)-(f-f^{*})\circ g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}\\ &\leq 2L_{\mathcal{F}}\cdot\|g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z)-g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}\\ &\leq 2L_{\mathcal{F}}L_{g,1}\cdot\|g_{t-1}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z)-g_{t-1}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z^{\prime})\|_{2}\\ &\leq 2L_{\mathcal{F}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}L_{g,i}\cdot\|z-z^{\prime}\|_{2}\,.\end{split} (17)

Therefore, LG=2​Lℱ​max⁡∏i=1tt∈[T]⁡Lg,iL_{G}=2L_{\mathcal{F}}\max_{t\in[T]}\prod_{i=1}^{t}L_{g,i} in this case.

On the other hand, for any f,f′∈ℱf,f^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F} parametrized by θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime} respectively, and for any z∈𝔹r​(dx)z\in\mathbb{B}_{r}(d_{x}), we have gt∘⋯∘g1(z)∈𝔹r′(dx)g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z)\in\mathbb{B}_{r^{\prime}}(d_{x}) and thus

supz∈𝔹r​(dx)‖Gf,t​(z)−Gf′,t​(z)‖2\displaystyle\sup_{z\in\mathbb{B}_{r}(d_{x})}\|G_{f,t}(z)-G_{f^{\prime},t}(z)\|_{2} =supz∈𝔹r​(dx)∥fθ∘gt∘⋯∘g1(z)−fθ′∘gt∘⋯∘g1(z)∥2\displaystyle=\sup_{z\in\mathbb{B}_{r}(d_{x})}\|f_{\theta}\circ g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z)-f_{\theta^{\prime}}\circ g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(z)\|_{2}
≤‖fθ−fθ′‖ℱ\displaystyle\leq\|f_{\theta}-f_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{\mathcal{F}}

Finally, to bound |‖Gf,t​(z)‖22−‖Gf′,t​(z)‖22|\left|\|G_{f,t}(z)\|_{2}^{2}-\|G_{f^{\prime},t}(z)\|_{2}^{2}\right|, let us define

Cmax=max{supθ∈Θ∥fθ∘gt∘⋯∘g1(0)∥2,∥f∗∘gt∘⋯∘g1(0)∥2}.\displaystyle C_{\max}=\max\biggl\{\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|f_{\theta}\circ g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(0)\|_{2},\|f^{*}\circ g_{t}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}(0)\|_{2}\biggl\}.

Since Θ\Theta is bounded, supθ∈Θ∥fθ∘gt∘⋯∘g1(0)∥2\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|f_{\theta}\!\circ\!g_{t}\!\circ\!\cdots\!\circ\!g_{1}(0)\|_{2} is finite, and thus CmaxC_{\max} is a finite constant. It then follows from the triangular inequality and Eq. 17 that

‖Gf,t​(z)‖2≤‖Gf,t​(z)−Gf,t​(0)‖2+‖Gf,t​(z)‖2≤LG⋅‖z‖2+Cmax.\displaystyle\|G_{f,t}(z)\|_{2}\leq\|G_{f,t}(z)-G_{f,t}(0)\|_{2}+\|G_{f,t}(z)\|_{2}\leq L_{G}\cdot\|z\|_{2}+C_{\max}.

We then obtain

supz∈𝔹r​(dx)|‖Gf,t​(z)‖22−‖Gf′,t​(z)‖22|\displaystyle\sup_{z\in\mathbb{B}_{r}(d_{x})}\left|\|G_{f,t}(z)\|_{2}^{2}-\|G_{f^{\prime},t}(z)\|_{2}^{2}\right|
≤\displaystyle\leq supz∈𝔹r​(dx)‖Gf,t​(z)−Gf′,t​(z)‖2⋅‖Gf,t​(z)+Gf′,t​(z)‖2\displaystyle\sup_{z\in\mathbb{B}_{r}(d_{x})}\|G_{f,t}(z)-G_{f^{\prime},t}(z)\|_{2}\cdot\|G_{f,t}(z)+G_{f^{\prime},t}(z)\|_{2}
≤\displaystyle\leq supz∈𝔹r​(dx)‖f−f′‖ℱ⋅(2​LG⋅‖z‖2+2​Cmax)\displaystyle\sup_{z\in\mathbb{B}_{r}(d_{x})}\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}\cdot\left(2L_{G}\cdot\|z\|_{2}+2C_{\max}\right)
=\displaystyle= ‖f−f′‖ℱ⋅(2​r​LG+2​Cmax)\displaystyle\ \|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}\cdot\left(2rL_{G}+2C_{\max}\right)

Set KG=max⁡(1,2​r​LG+2​Cmax)K_{G}=\max\left(1,2rL_{G}+2C_{\max}\right) and we finish the proof. ∎

B.1 Proposition 1 and Its Proof

Proposition 1.

Fix u>0u>0. Let CC be some constant larger than 11, and write wavg:=1T​∑t∈[T]wtw_{\text{avg}}:=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}w_{t}. Recall the quadratic term Q⁡(f,C)Q(f,C) defined in Eq. 26:

Bsq:=supf∈ℱ|𝔼⁡[1T​∑t∈[T]wt​(‖G~f,t​(x1)‖22−‖Gf,t​(x1)‖22)]|.B_{\text{sq}}:=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}w_{t}\left(\|\tilde{G}_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}-\|G_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right)\right]\right|. (39)

Let ℱ⁡(ε)\mathcal{F}(\varepsilon) be the smallest ε\varepsilon-net of ℱ\{f∗}\mathcal{F}\ \backslash\{f^{*}\}, then we have

ℙ(Q(f,C)>2Bsq+(C+1)wavgKGε2,∀f∈ℱ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(Q(f,C)>2B_{\text{sq}}+(C+1)w_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\varepsilon^{2},\forall f\in\mathcal{F}\right) ≤|ℱ⁡(ε)|⋅𝖾𝗑𝗉⁡(−(C−1)​mint∈[T]​nt2​C2​κ2)\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathcal{F}(\varepsilon)\right|\cdot{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{(C-1)\min_{t\in[T]}n_{t}}{2C^{2}\kappa^{2}}\right)
+m⋅𝖾𝗑𝗉(−dx​(rx−2​σ)2128​σ2).\displaystyle\ \ +m\cdot{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{d_{x}(r_{x}-2\sigma)^{2}}{128\sigma^{2}}\right).
Proof.

For any f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, let f′∈ℱ⁡(ε)f^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}(\varepsilon) be such that ‖f′−f‖ℱ≤ε\|f^{\prime}-f\|_{\mathcal{F}}\leq\varepsilon. It follows from Assumption 4 that

𝔼⁡[1T​∑t∈[T]wt⋅(‖G~f,t​(x1)‖22−‖G~f′,t​(x1)‖22)]≤wavg​KG​‖f−f′‖ℱ2;CT​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt⋅(‖G~f′,t​(x1)‖22−‖G~f,t​(x1)‖22)≤C​wavg​KG​‖f−f′‖ℱ2.\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}w_{t}\cdot\left(\|\tilde{G}_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}-\|\tilde{G}_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right)\right]&\leq w_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}^{2};\\ \frac{C}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in{\cal M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\cdot\left(\|\tilde{G}_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}-\|\tilde{G}_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right)&\leq Cw_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}^{2}.\end{split} (40)

(41)

Q⁡(f,C)\displaystyle Q(f,C) =1T​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt​(𝔼⁡[‖Gf,t​(x1)‖22]−C⋅‖Gf,t​(x1​i)‖22)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\|G_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]-C\cdot\|G_{f,t}(x_{1i})\|_{2}^{2}\right)
≤(i)​Bsq+1T​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt​(𝔼⁡[‖G~f,t​(x1)‖22]−C⋅‖Gf,t​(x1​i)‖22)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(i)}}{\leq}B_{\text{sq}}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\|\tilde{G}_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]-C\cdot\|G_{f,t}(x_{1i})\|_{2}^{2}\right)
≤(ii)​Bsq+1T​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt​(𝔼⁡[‖G~f,t​(x1)‖22]−C⋅‖G~f,t​(x1​i)‖22)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(ii)}}{\leq}B_{\text{sq}}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\|\tilde{G}_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]-C\cdot\|\tilde{G}_{f,t}(x_{1i})\|_{2}^{2}\right)
≤(iii)​Bsq+1T​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt​(𝔼⁡[‖G~f′,t​(x1)‖22]−C⋅‖G~f′,t​(x1​i)‖22)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(iii)}}{\leq}B_{\text{sq}}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\|\tilde{G}_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]-C\cdot\|\tilde{G}_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1i})\|_{2}^{2}\right)
+(C+1)​wavg​KG​‖f−f′‖ℱ2\displaystyle\quad+(C+1)w_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}^{2}
≤(iv)​Bsq+1T​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt​(𝔼⁡[‖G~f′,t​(x1)‖22]−C⋅‖Gf′,t​(x1​i)‖22)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(iv)}}{\leq}B_{\text{sq}}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\|\tilde{G}_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]-C\cdot\|G_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1i})\|_{2}^{2}\right)
+(C+1)​wavg​KG​‖f−f′‖ℱ2\displaystyle\quad+(C+1)w_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}^{2}
≤(v)​2​Bsq+1T​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt​(𝔼⁡[‖Gf′,t​(x1)‖22]−C⋅‖Gf′,t​(x1​i)‖22)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(v)}}{\leq}2B_{\text{sq}}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\|G_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]-C\cdot\|G_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1i})\|_{2}^{2}\right)
+(C+1)​wavg​KG​‖f−f′‖ℱ2\displaystyle\quad+(C+1)w_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}^{2}
≤(vi)​2​Bsq+(C+1)​wavg​KG​‖f−f′‖ℱ2\displaystyle\overset{\text{(vi)}}{\leq}2B_{\text{sq}}+(C+1)w_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\|f-f^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{F}}^{2}
≤(vii)​2​Bsq+(C+1)​wavg​KG​ε2.\displaystyle\overset{\text{(vii)}}{\leq}2B_{\text{sq}}+(C+1)w_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\varepsilon^{2}.

Here, (i) follows from the definitions of BsqB_{\text{sq}} and Q⁡(f,C)Q(f,C), (iii) follows by summing the two inequalities in Eq. 40 and rearranging, (ii) and (iv) follow from the event x1​i≤rxx_{1i}\leq r_{x} (∀i∈[m]\forall i\in[m]), which implies Gf,t​(x1​i)=G~f,t​(x1​i)G_{f,t}(x_{1i})=\tilde{G}_{f,t}(x_{1i}) and Gf′,t​(x1​i)=G~f′,t​(x1​i)G_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1i})=\tilde{G}_{f^{\prime},t}(x_{1i}), (v) follows again from the definition of BsqB_{\text{sq}}, (vi) follows from the event that Eq. 41 holds, and (vii) follows from the definition of the ε\varepsilon-net ℱ⁡(ε)\mathcal{F}(\varepsilon).

ℙ(Q(f,C)>2Bsq+(C+1)wavgKGε2,∀f∈ℱ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(Q(f,C)>2B_{\text{sq}}+(C+1)w_{\text{avg}}K_{G}\varepsilon^{2},\forall f\in\mathcal{F}\right) ≤|ℱ⁡(ε)|⋅𝖾𝗑𝗉⁡(−(C−1)​mint∈[T]​nt2​C2​κ2)\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathcal{F}(\varepsilon)\right|\cdot{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{(C-1)\min_{t\in[T]}n_{t}}{2C^{2}\kappa^{2}}\right)

Lemma 2.

Recall the definition of κ\kappa in Eq. 8:

κ=supf∈ℱ\{f∗}supt∈[T],wt>0𝔼​[‖Gf,t​(x1)‖24]1/2𝔼⁡[‖Gf,t​(x1)‖22].\kappa=\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}\ \backslash\{f^{*}\}}\sup_{t\in[T],w_{t}>0}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\|G_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{4}\right]^{1/2}}{\mathbb{E}\left[\|G_{f,t}(x_{1})\|_{2}^{2}\right]}.

For any fixed f∈ℱ\{f∗}f\in\mathcal{F}\ \backslash\{f^{*}\} and C>1C>1 we have

𝔼⁡[1T​∑t∈[T]wt⋅‖f⁡(xt)−f∗​(xt)‖22]≤CT​∑(t,i)∈ℳwtnt⋅‖f∗​(xt​i)−f⁡(xt​i)‖22\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}w_{t}\cdot\|f(x_{t})-f^{*}(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{C}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\cdot\|f^{*}(x_{ti})-f(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}

with probability at least

1−𝖾𝗑𝗉⁡(−(C−1)​mint∈[T],wt>0​nt2​C2​κ2).\displaystyle 1-{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{(C-1)\min_{t\in[T],w_{t}>0}n_{t}}{2C^{2}\kappa^{2}}\right).
Proof.

In the proof we assume wt>0w_{t}>0 for all t∈[T]t\in[T], as the case with some of the wtw_{t}’s being zero follows immediately. Define F:=f−f∗F:=f-f^{*}. Then we need to compute the probability of the event

{𝔼[1T∑t∈[T]wt⋅∥F(xt)∥22]≤CT∑(t,i)∈ℳwt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22nt},\displaystyle\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\in[T]}w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\frac{C}{T}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{t}}\right\}, (42)

or equivalently

{𝔼[∑t∈[T]wt⋅∥F(xt)∥22]≤C⋅∑(t,i)∈ℳwt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22nt}.\displaystyle\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t\in[T]}w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq C\cdot\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{t}}\right\}. (43)

Applying the Chernoff-Cramér bound gives

ℙ⁡(C​∑(t,i)∈ℳwt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22nt≤∑t∈[T]𝔼⁡[wt⋅‖F⁡(xt)‖22])\displaystyle\ \mathbb{P}\left(C\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{t}}\leq\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq infα>0𝖾𝗑𝗉(α⋅∑t∈[T]𝔼[wt⋅∥F(xt)∥22])⋅𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(−α⋅C∑(t,i)∈ℳwt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22nt)].\displaystyle\ \inf_{\alpha>0}{\mathsf{exp}}\left(\alpha\cdot\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]\right)\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\alpha\cdot C\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{t}}\right)\right].

We proceed by bounding the rightmost term:

𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(−α⋅C∑(t,i)∈ℳwt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22nt)]\displaystyle\ \mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\alpha\cdot C\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{t}}\right)\right]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(−Cα∑i∈[m]∑t∈ℳiwt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22nt)]\displaystyle\ \mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-C\alpha\sum_{i\in[m]}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}\frac{w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{t}}\right)\right]
=(i)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(i)}}{=} ∏i∈[m]𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(−Cα∑t∈ℳiwt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22nt)]\displaystyle\ \prod_{i\in[m]}\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-C\alpha\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}\frac{w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{t}}\right)\right]
≤(ii)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(ii)}}{\leq} ∏i∈[m]𝖾𝗑𝗉(−Cα∑t∈ℳi𝔼⁡[wt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22]nt+C2​α22κ2(∑t∈ℳi𝔼⁡[wt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22]nt)2)\displaystyle\ \prod_{i\in[m]}{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-C\alpha\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}\right]}{n_{t}}+\frac{C^{2}\alpha^{2}}{2}\kappa^{2}\left(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}\right]}{n_{t}}\right)^{2}\right)
=\displaystyle= 𝖾𝗑𝗉(−Cα∑t∈[T]𝔼[wt⋅∥F(xt)∥22]+C2​α22κ2∑i∈[m](∑t∈ℳi𝔼⁡[wt⋅‖F⁡(xt)‖22]nt)2)\displaystyle\ {\mathsf{exp}}\left(-C\alpha\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]+\frac{C^{2}\alpha^{2}}{2}\kappa^{2}\sum_{i\in[m]}\left(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\right]}{n_{t}}\right)^{2}\right)
≤(iii)\displaystyle\overset{\text{(iii)}}{\leq} 𝖾𝗑𝗉(−Cα∑t∈[T]𝔼[wt⋅∥F(xt)∥22]+C2​α2​κ22​mint∈[T]​nt(∑t∈[T]𝔼[wt⋅∥F(xt)∥22])2)\displaystyle\ {\mathsf{exp}}\left(-C\alpha\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]+\frac{C^{2}\alpha^{2}\kappa^{2}}{2\min_{t\in[T]}n_{t}}\left(\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]\right)^{2}\right)

where (i) follows from the assumption that the data indexed by ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} are i.i.d., and therefore the trajectories are independent (Lemma 7), (ii) follows from Lemma 10, and (iii) follows from Lemma 11. Combining the above gives

ℙ⁡(C​∑(t,i)∈ℳwt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22nt≤∑t∈[T]𝔼⁡[wt⋅‖F⁡(xt)‖22])\displaystyle\ \mathbb{P}\left(C\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{M}}\frac{w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}}{n_{t}}\leq\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq 𝖾𝗑𝗉(−(C−1)α∑t∈[T]𝔼[wt⋅∥F(xt)∥22]+C2​α2​κ22​mint∈[T]​nt(∑t∈[T]𝔼[wt⋅∥F(xt)∥22])2).\displaystyle\ {\mathsf{exp}}\left(-(C-1)\alpha\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]+\frac{C^{2}\alpha^{2}\kappa^{2}}{2\min_{t\in[T]}n_{t}}\left(\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]\right)^{2}\right).

Since the above holds for any α>0\alpha>0, we take

α=C−1C2​∑t∈[T]𝔼⁡[wt⋅‖F⁡(xt)‖22]⋅mint∈[T]⁡ntκ2\displaystyle\alpha=\frac{C-1}{C^{2}\sum_{t\in[T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[w_{t}\cdot\|F(x_{t})\|_{2}^{2}\Big]}\cdot\frac{\min_{t\in[T]}n_{t}}{\kappa^{2}}

and plugging this value back we obtain the desired result. ∎

Lemma 3 (Projection Difference).

Let z=[z1,…,zd]⊤z=[z_{1},\dots,z_{d}]^{\top} be a sub-Gaussian vector with proxy variance σ2/d\sigma^{2}/d and independent coordinates. Let hh be a vector-valued function that is Lipschitz continuous with constant LL. For any r>2​σr>2\sigma we have

𝔼⁡[‖h⁡(𝒫𝔹r​(d)​(z))−h⁡(z)‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|h(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)}(z))-h(z)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right] ≤L2​(128​σ2d+2⋅642​σ4d2​(r−2​σ)2)​𝖾𝗑𝗉​(−d​(r−2​σ)2128​σ2).\displaystyle\leq L^{2}\left(\frac{128\sigma^{2}}{d}+\frac{2\cdot 64^{2}\sigma^{4}}{d^{2}(r-2\sigma)^{2}}\right){\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{d(r-2\sigma)^{2}}{128\sigma^{2}}\right).

Furthermore, if r>3​σr>3\sigma, then we have σ2/(r−2​σ)2≤1\sigma^{2}/(r-2\sigma)^{2}\leq 1 and thus

𝔼⁡[‖h⁡(𝒫𝔹r​(d)​(z))−h⁡(z)‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|h(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)}(z))-h(z)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right] ≤128​L2​σ2d2​(d+64)​𝖾𝗑𝗉​(−d​(r−2​σ)2128​σ2).\displaystyle\leq 128\frac{L^{2}\sigma^{2}}{d^{2}}(d+64){\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{d(r-2\sigma)^{2}}{128\sigma^{2}}\right).
Proof.

Since hh is LL-Lipschitz, we have

𝔼⁡[‖h⁡(𝒫𝔹r​(d)​(z))−h⁡(z)‖22]≤L2⋅𝔼⁡[‖𝒫𝔹r​(d)​(z)−z‖22],\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|h(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)}(z))-h(z)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq L^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)}(z)-z\right\|_{2}^{2}\right],

and therefore it remains to bound the expectation 𝔼⁡[‖𝒫𝔹r​(d)​(z)−z‖22]\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)}(z)-z\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. If z∈𝔹r​(d)z\in\mathbb{B}_{r}(d), then we have this expectation equal to 00. Hence we only need to consider z∉𝔹r​(d)z\notin\mathbb{B}_{r}(d), which means

𝔼⁡[‖𝒫𝔹r​(d)​(z)−z‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)}(z)-z\right\|_{2}^{2}\right] =𝔼⁡[‖𝒫𝔹r​(d)​(z)−z‖22|z∉𝔹r​(d)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)}(z)-z\right\|_{2}^{2}\ \big|\ z\notin\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)\right]
=𝔼⁡[‖r⋅z‖z‖2−z‖22|z∉𝔹r​(d)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|r\cdot\frac{z}{\|z\|_{2}}-z\right\|_{2}^{2}\ \big|\ z\notin\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)\right]
=𝔼⁡[|r−‖z‖2|2|z∉𝔹r​(d)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left|r-\|z\|_{2}\right|^{2}\ \big|\ z\notin\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)\right]

Applying the Integral Identity (Lemma 20) with some basic probability calculation yields

=∫0∞ℙ⁡(‖z‖2−r>τ|z∉𝔹r​(d))​𝑑τ\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(\|z\|_{2}-r>\sqrt{\tau}\ \big|\ z\notin\mathbb{B}_{r}(d)\right)\ d\tau
≤∫0∞ℙ⁡(‖z‖2−r>τ)​𝑑τ\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(\|z\|_{2}-r>\sqrt{\tau}\right)\ d\tau

Lemma 4.

Consider the ball 𝔹rx​(dx)\mathbb{B}_{r_{x}}(d_{x}) in ℝdx\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} of radius rxr_{x} with rx>3​σr_{x}>3\sigma, and recall that 𝒫𝔹rx​(dx)\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{B}_{r_{x}}(d_{x})} denotes projection onto 𝔹rx​(dx)\mathbb{B}_{r_{x}}(d_{x}). Bsq​(rx)≤128​wavg​LG2​σ2dx2​(dx+64)​𝖾𝗑𝗉​(−dx​(rx−2​σ)2128​σ2)+16​wavg​LG​σdx​2​M2​(dx+64)​𝖾𝗑𝗉​(−dx​(rx−2​σ)2256​σ2).\displaystyle\begin{split}B_{\text{sq}}(r_{x})&\leq 128w_{\text{avg}}\frac{L_{G}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{d_{x}^{2}}(d_{x}+64){\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{d_{x}(r_{x}-2\sigma)^{2}}{128\sigma^{2}}\right)\\ &\ +16w_{\text{avg}}\frac{L_{G}\sigma}{d_{x}}\sqrt{2M_{2}(d_{x}+64)}{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{d_{x}(r_{x}-2\sigma)^{2}}{256\sigma^{2}}\right).\end{split} (44)

+16​LG​σdx​2​M2​(dx+64)​𝖾𝗑𝗉​(−dx​(r−2​σ)2256​σ2).\displaystyle\ +16\frac{L_{G}\sigma}{d_{x}}\sqrt{2M_{2}(d_{x}+64)}{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-\frac{d_{x}(r-2\sigma)^{2}}{256\sigma^{2}}\right).

Lemma 5.

Fix f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}. Recall that M⁡(f)M(f) is defined in Eq. 25 as

we need to prove ℙ⁡(M⁡(f)≥u)≤𝖾𝗑𝗉⁡(−u​a)\mathbb{P}\left(M(f)\geq u\right)\leq{\mathsf{exp}}\left(-ua\right). Since Markov’s inequality implies

For any fixed f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, write F:=f−f∗F:=f-f^{*}. Note that vt​iv_{ti} is conditioned on x1​i,…,xt​ix_{1i},\dots,x_{ti} is sub-Gaussian, thus, for any (t,i)∈ℳ(t,i)\in\mathcal{M} we have

𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(aT⋅wtnt[4⋅⟨vt​i,F(xt​i)⟩−∥F(xt​i)∥22])|x1​i,…,xt​i]≤(i)𝖾𝗑𝗉⁡(ν22⋅16​a2​wt2T2​nt2​‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22−a​wtT​nt⋅‖F⁡(xt​i)‖22)≤(ii) 1,\begin{split}&\ \mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(\frac{a}{T}\cdot\frac{w_{t}}{n_{t}}\left[4\cdot\langle v_{ti},F(x_{ti})\rangle-\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}\right]\right)\ \big|\ x_{1i},\dots,x_{ti}\right]\\ \overset{\text{(i)}}{\leq}&\ {\mathsf{exp}}\left(\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{16a^{2}w_{t}^{2}}{T^{2}n_{t}^{2}}\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}-\frac{aw_{t}}{Tn_{t}}\cdot\|F(x_{ti})\|_{2}^{2}\right)\\ \overset{\text{(ii)}}{\leq}&\ 1,\end{split} (47)

where (i) follows from the property of sub-Gaussian vectors vt​iv_{ti} as shown in Eq. 72, and (ii) follows from the definition of aa, that is a≤T8​ν2⋅ntwta\leq\frac{T}{8\nu^{2}}\cdot\frac{n_{t}}{w_{t}}, which implies ν22​T⋅16​a2​wt2T2​nt2−a​wtT​nt≤0\frac{\nu^{2}}{2T}\cdot\frac{16a^{2}w_{t}^{2}}{T^{2}n_{t}^{2}}-\frac{aw_{t}}{Tn_{t}}\leq 0. and write X1:t:={x1​i,…,xt​i}i∈[m]X_{1:t}:=\{x_{1i},\dots,x_{ti}\}_{i\in[m]}. Since for any i∈ℛti\in\mathcal{R}_{t} we have that vt​iv_{ti}’s are independent of each other, from Eq. 47 it follows that

Note that a⋅M⁡(f)=∑t∈[T]Rta\cdot M(f)=\sum_{t\in[T]}R_{t}, and we have

𝔼⁡[𝖾𝗑𝗉⁡(a⋅M⁡(f))]=𝔼⁡[𝖾𝗑𝗉⁡(∑t∈[T]Rt)]=(i)𝔼[𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(∑t∈[T]Rt)|X1:T]]=(ii)𝔼[𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(∑t∈[T−1]Rt)|X1:T]]⋅𝔼[𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(RT)|X1:T]]≤(iii)𝔼[𝔼[𝖾𝗑𝗉(∑t∈[T−1]Rt)|X1:T]]=(iv)​𝔼​[𝖾𝗑𝗉⁡(∑t∈[T−1]Rt)]≤⋯≤1.\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(a\cdot M(f)\right)\right]&=\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(\sum_{t\in[T]}R_{t}\right)\right]\\ &\overset{\text{(i)}}{=}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(\sum_{t\in[T]}R_{t}\right)\ \big|\ X_{1:T}\right]\right]\\ &\overset{\text{(ii)}}{=}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(\sum_{t\in[T-1]}R_{t}\right)\ \big|\ X_{1:T}\right]\right]\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(R_{T}\right)\ \big|\ X_{1:T}\right]\right]\\ &\overset{\text{(iii)}}{\leq}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(\sum_{t\in[T-1]}R_{t}\right)\ \big|\ X_{1:T}\right]\right]\\ &\overset{\text{(iv)}}{=}\mathbb{E}\left[{\mathsf{exp}}\left(\sum_{t\in[T-1]}R_{t}\right)\right]\\ &\leq\cdots\leq 1.\end{split} (49)

Above, (i) and (iv) follow from the law of total expectation, (ii) follows from the fact that vT​iv_{Ti}’s are independent of other noise vectors vt​iv_{ti}’s when conditioned on X1:TX_{1:T}, and (iii) follows from Eq. 48, and the rest of the derivations follows a recursive application of the previous steps. ∎
